ta-l1d40q2-d1e100.summary: The second question of Distinction 40 asks of whom predestination is, with a first argument that it is only of existing things: predestination signifies a kind of sending, and only what exists is sent.
claims: Only the existent can be sent.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e103.summary: Second argument. What does not exist cannot be prepared for anything, and predestination is a preparation.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e106.summary: Third argument that it is not of angels. Predestination is the purpose of having mercy (Augustine), and angels were never wretched, and mercy regards wretchedness.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e110.summary: Fourth argument that it is not of the blessed in glory. What is at its last end cannot be directed to it, and the blessed are at theirs.
claims: The blessed are at their end.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e113.summary: Fifth argument that it is not of the Son of God. Predestination implies precedence, like foreknowledge, and none can be designated with respect to the eternal Son.
claims: No precedence to the eternal Son.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e116.summary: Contrary argument that it is of all humans. God relates equally to all (Dionysius), so if he prepares grace for some, he does for all.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e119.summary: Second contrary argument. As we are directed to goods of grace by God, so to goods of nature, which he gives to good and bad (Matt. 5), and predestination is direction to an end, the good.
claims: God gives natural goods to all.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e122.summary: Thomas's determination. Predestination is said to be of things in two ways: of the end and what leads to it, grace and glory; and of those who attain the end, all who reach glory through God's grace. Both follow from the name, which joins the act of destining with 'prae'. 'To destine' signifies directing something to something, as a messenger; it also means purposing (2 Macc. 6:20, Eleazar destined not to admit what was unlawful), derived from the first, since what is purposed is directed to execution. Properly something is directed to what it has nothing in itself to reach, so predestination properly concerns what humans cannot attain by their natural powers, grace and glory (Damascene: predestination is of what is not in us). So whatever cannot attain grace and glory is not predestined; only those who will attain glory through grace are. 'Prae' implies precedence, which belongs differently to different subjects: in human predestination there is precedence of eternity to nature, nature to grace, and grace to glory; in angels, of eternity to nature and nature to grace (for those holding angels were created in natural endowments only) but not of grace to glory in duration, or, for those holding angels were created in grace, of grace to glory but not nature to grace; in Christ, not of eternity to the person but only to the other nature, nor of nature to grace, nor of grace to glory as to enjoyment, but only as to the soul's impassibility and the body's endowments. So predestination fits different subjects differently.
claims: Predestination is of grace and glory as end and means, and of those who attain glory through grace.
It concerns what exceeds natural powers; its precedence varies for humans, angels, and Christ.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first argument. Those who neither are nor will be are not predestined, but those who will be, though they are not, whom God knows by knowledge of vision, are; though not actually directed as existing in their own nature, they are pre-directed to the end as in God's foreknowledge.
claims: Future persons are pre-directed as known by vision.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e132.summary: Reply to the second argument. Preparation is twofold: of matter, disposed to receive form, which applies only to the existent; and of the agent, to act, as a natural agent acquires a disposition and an artisan conceives the form and purposes to execute it, and such preparation is in God even regarding future things.
claims: God's preparation is that of an agent, not of matter.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e135.summary: Reply to the third argument. That definition concerns predestination as regarding the present state of wretchedness, not absolutely. Or 'having mercy' is taken not for removing prior wretchedness but for conferring that without which there would be wretchedness, especially what is conferred by gratuitous will alone.
claims: Mercy can mean conferring what prevents misery.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e138.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Predestined' taken participially co-signifies past time, and so those in heaven are predestined, since what is once past is always past; taken neutrally, they can be called predestined only as directed to continuance of beatitude, which is improper, since it has no extension of succession.
claims: The blessed are predestined in the past-tense sense.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Though no precedence can be designated with respect to the Son's person absolutely, it can with respect to the human nature or to the person as subsisting in it; this is treated more in III, Dist. 2.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the first contrary argument. Though God in himself relates equally to all, not all relate equally to him, so grace is not prepared equally for all.
claims: Inequality is on the creatures' side.

ta-l1d40q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the second contrary argument. Predestination properly concerns what is raised above natural capacity, so it is not of all who receive natural goods from God but of those for whom grace and glory are prepared.

ta-l1d40q2-Dd1e92.summary: The single article of the second question of Distinction 40 holds that predestination is of grace and glory as end and means, and of those who will attain glory through grace, since it concerns what exceeds natural powers. Its precedence differs for humans, angels, and Christ. Future persons are pre-directed as known by vision, God's preparation is an agent's, the blessed are predestined in the past-tense sense, Christ is predestined as man, and grace is unequal because creatures relate unequally to God.
claims: Predestination is of grace and glory and of those who attain glory by grace.

ta-l1d40q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 40 asks of whom predestination is. Thomas holds that it concerns grace and glory, which exceed natural powers, and those who will attain glory through grace, including future persons known by vision, angels, and Christ as man, with different orders of precedence. It is not of all humans, since creatures relate unequally to God.
claims: Predestination is of those who will attain glory through grace.
